core: placing not after be, modal, and auxiliary verbs to form negative statements
do-support: borrowing the auxiliary do when no auxiliary exists (She does not work; She doesn't work)
negative contractions and their full forms: isn't, aren't, don't, doesn't, didn't, won't, can't
negative words: never, no, nothing, nobody, nowhere, neither
the single-negation rule of standard written English, with the two-negative pattern described neutrally as a dialect and register difference
negative questions introduced and named briefly (Don't you like it?), with full question formation left to the questions lesson
common learner errors: double negatives in formal writing, no versus not confusion, missing do-support
supporting: register contrast between contractions (speech and informal writing) and full forms (formal writing and emphasis)
the irregular forms won't (will not) and cannot (can + not)
no before a noun phrase versus not with verbs and other phrases
neither as a determiner and in neither ... nor
negative imperatives (Do not open; Don't take the car)

negative adverbs such as hardly, seldom, and rarely

claims.claim: Negative statements are formed by placing not (or n't) after be, after modal verbs, and after the auxiliary verbs do and have; the main verb keeps its normal form.
When a sentence has no auxiliary or modal verb, English adds the auxiliary do (do-support) to carry the negation, as in "She does not work" and "She doesn't work."

n't is the contracted form of not and attaches without a space to be, modal verbs, and the auxiliaries do and have; the contracted form of will not is won't, and the uncontracted form of can plus not is cannot.

Negative contractions include isn't, aren't, wasn't, weren't, don't, doesn't, didn't, hasn't, haven't, can't, couldn't, won't, and shouldn't; contractions are common in everyday speech and informal writing, while formal writing prefers full forms.

Standard English does not use two negatives in the same clause; words such as never, nobody, no one, none, nothing, and nowhere already carry a negative meaning, so a clause containing one needs no second negative, and not pairs with any-words instead.

Some speakers use two negatives in the same clause, and many people consider this incorrect; the lesson teaches the standard written convention of one negative per clause while describing the spoken variation neutrally, without labeling any community deficient.
No is used before a noun phrase, while not is used with verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and other phrases.

Neither makes a negative statement about two people or things, appears before singular countable nouns and as neither of before pronouns and plural noun phrases, and can pair with nor to connect two negative alternatives.

Negative questions are formed with not or n't after be or a modal, and with do plus n't when no other auxiliary is present (Don't you like it?); full question formation belongs to the questions lesson.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Double negatives in a single clause
positions: Standard written English does not have two negatives in the same clause; a negative word such as never, nothing, or nobody already makes the clause negative (Cambridge Grammar, 'Negation: two negatives').
Some speakers use two negatives in the same clause, and many people consider this incorrect; the same Cambridge source notes the pattern is heard from some speakers.

The subject source-map caution requires describing language choices as context-sensitive and distinguishing formal conventions, regional varieties, and communicative goals without labeling learners deficient.
Some English varieties use multiple negation systematically as a feature of the variety, which the lesson acknowledges neutrally as a real spoken pattern.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches one negative per clause as the convention of standard written English, notes that the two-negative pattern appears in some spoken varieties and is a real, describable pattern rather than a personal failing, and advises full forms plus single negation for formal writing.

sourceRecords.title: Not — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar (English Grammar Today)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: not as the most common negation word; negative declarative clauses formed with not after be, modals, and auxiliaries do and have; n't as the contracted form attached without a space; no n't form with am and may (I'm not, We may not); won't for will not and cannot for can plus not; negative questions using do + n't when no other auxiliary exists; full form not for formal writing or emphasis. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Forming negative statements, questions and imperatives — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar (English Grammar Today)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: negative statements formed with not or n't after be, modal, and auxiliary verbs; n't attachable to be, modals (except may), and auxiliaries do and have; won't as the negative contracted form of will and cannot as the uncontracted form of can plus not; negative questions using auxiliary do + n't when no modal or be is present (don't, do not, doesn't, does not, didn't); negative imperatives with do not or don't plus the base form. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Negation: two negatives — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar (English Grammar Today)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: standard English does not have two negatives in the same clause; never, nobody, no one, none, nothing, nowhere already have a negative meaning so no second negative is needed with the verb; with not, use ever, anybody, anyone, anything, anywhere instead; the source notes some speakers use two negatives in the same clause and many people consider this incorrect. The lesson teaches the standard convention while describing the variation neutrally. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: No or not? — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar (English Grammar Today)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: no is used before a noun phrase (There's no address on the envelope; No decisions have been made) while not is used with any other phrase or clause; no + noun can be stronger than not + any; no is used to respond to a yes-no question while not is not used alone that way. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Neither, neither … nor and not … either — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar (English Grammar Today)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: neither allows a negative statement about two people or things at the same time and goes before singular countable nouns; neither of appears before pronouns and plural countable nouns with a determiner; neither ... nor connects two or more negative alternatives and can sound formal. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
